questions.question: Trofim Lysenko, a Soviet agronomist, soaked and chilled winter wheat seed so that it could be sown in spring and still bear grain that summer, a treatment called vernalisation. He went further than the plants he treated: he claimed that the change would be inherited. Which result would have borne out that claim?
questions.answer: Seed of chilled plants, sown unchilled in spring, bearing grain
choices: Seed of chilled plants, sown unchilled in spring, bearing grain
Chilled seed, sown in spring, bearing grain the same summer
Chilled seed giving a bigger harvest than unchilled seed
Unchilled winter wheat, sown in spring, bearing no grain that summer
questions.context: Only the offspring of chilled plants, sown in spring with no cold of their own, could show a change passed down; the other results tell only what cold does to the seed it touches, or what winter wheat does without it. Plant biologists have since found that the chilled state is wiped clean as each new embryo forms, so every generation needs its own winter. Nikolai Vavilov, the country's leading plant scientist, at first encouraged Lysenko's work and stopped when it failed to deliver.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks which result would test a claim, and an inherited change can only be tested in the offspring, not in the plant that was treated.

questions.question: Trofim Lysenko denied that genes existed and rejected Gregor Mendel's laws of heredity. N. I. Ermolaeva, one of his followers, repeated some of Mendel's pea crosses and reported in 1939 that the hybrids' offspring did not keep to Mendel's ratio of 3 to 1. The mathematician Andrey Kolmogorov went through her counts in 1940. What did he find?
questions.answer: They strayed from 3 to 1 only as far as chance allows
choices: They strayed from 3 to 1 only as far as chance allows
They kept closer to a ratio of 1 to 1 than to 3 to 1
They showed the parents' traits blending in the offspring
They showed traits that the parent plants had acquired
questions.context: Real counts never land exactly on 3 to 1, any more than a hundred coin tosses land exactly fifty-fifty, and Kolmogorov showed that her counts scattered around Mendel's ratio just as chance predicts, calling them a new confirmation of Mendel's laws. Lysenko held that Kolmogorov was wrong; he dismissed statistical treatment of data as 'bourgeois formalism'. Two researchers who rechecked the work in 2011 found flaws in Kolmogorov's method, yet a corrected test still confirmed his conclusion.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that measurements vary by chance and that data are judged against that variation, not against an exact figure.

questions.question: Joseph Stalin approved the session of the Lenin All-Union Academy of Agricultural Sciences in Moscow in August 1948, where Trofim Lysenko spoke against the geneticists. On the last day Lysenko told the hall that the Communist Party's Central Committee had examined his report and approved it. What became of genetics in the Soviet Union after the session?
questions.answer: It was barred from teaching and research
choices: It was barred from teaching and research
It was taught beside Lysenko's ideas as a rival
It was kept for animals but barred for crops
It was put to a public test in the fields
questions.context: Genetics was branded a 'bourgeois pseudoscience', more than 3,000 biologists were dismissed or jailed, and an order went out to destroy the fruit-fly stocks geneticists bred. Soviet leaders had wanted Lysenko's quick promises after the famine of the early 1930s, when breeding by genetics looked slow. The ban was lifted only in the mid-1960s, after his methods had failed in the fields and he lost his posts.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches that claims are settled by evidence and sceptical review, and the 1948 session is the standard case of a claim settled by power instead.

questions.question: Crews planting belts of forest across the Soviet steppes under a plan of 1948 sowed acorns in clusters by Trofim Lysenko's nest method. Lysenko held that plants of one kind do not compete with one another, and that seedlings crowded together in a 'nest' help one another grow. The ecologist Vladimir Sukachev followed the plantings in the Ural lands. What had become of those trees by September 1951?
questions.answer: Every tree sown that way had died
choices: Every tree sown that way had died
They had outgrown trees sown one by one
Most nests had kept just one strong tree
They had lived but grown too slowly to block wind
questions.context: Sukachev, an opponent of Lysenko, recorded that by September 1951 every tree planted by the nest method in the Ural lands had died. Seedlings of one kind need the same light, water and soil nutrients, so crowding them together sharpens their competition rather than ending it. Where a crowded stand does survive, it is because a few of the strongest take what the rest needed; in the Ural nests none survived at all.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade ecology teaches competition within a species for limited resources, and the nest plantings show a field result refuting a claim that denied it.

questions.question: Nikolai Vavilov, the Soviet Union's leading plant scientist, led expeditions to five continents in the 1920s and 1930s and built in Leningrad the world's largest collection of crop seeds. He sought out old local varieties and the wild relatives of crops, not only the best modern kinds. Why did he want those?
questions.answer: Their genes held traits breeders could cross into crops
choices: Their genes held traits breeders could cross into crops
They could be trained by cold to grow well on any farm
They stayed alive in storage far longer than modern seed
They gave bigger harvests than the modern varieties did
questions.context: Vavilov judged that modern crops, bred to be alike, were too uniform to withstand new diseases and hard seasons, while old local kinds and wild relatives hold the variety of genes, for traits such as resistance to drought and pests, that breeders can cross back in; he had wanted since boyhood to end famine. The secret police arrested him in 1940, while he was collecting seeds in Ukraine, for opposing Lysenko, and he died of starvation in Saratov prison in 1943. Through the siege of Leningrad his institute's staff guarded the collection, and some of them starved rather than eat it.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches genetic variation as the raw material of breeding and selection, and Vavilov's collection is the classic seed bank built on that idea.

questions.question: Charles Davenport's Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor, New York, sent field workers door to door from 1910 to chart family trees. Where 'feeblemindedness' or pauperism turned up in parents and their children, the office counted it as inherited, often through a single gene. What could such a family tree never sort out?
questions.answer: Whether genes or a shared home and upbringing caused it
choices: Whether genes or a shared home and upbringing caused it
Whether the trait passed through the mother or the father
Whether the trait skipped a generation and came back
Whether more sons than daughters showed the trait
questions.context: Davenport, funded by Mary Harriman and later the Carnegie Institution, treated human traits as Mendelian 'unit characters', as the new genetics seemed to allow; but a family shares its home, food, schooling and poverty as well as its genes, so a trait that runs in a family does not by itself show that genes carry it, and Davenport also studied the genetics of pellagra, which proved to come from a vitamin missing in the diet. Critics of the day, among them Thomas Hunt Morgan and Herbert Spencer Jennings, argued that he overlooked the surroundings and that most human traits depend on many genes. 'Feebleminded' was a loose label for many conditions with many causes, and intelligence is now known to be shaped by a great many genes, each with a small effect, as well as by upbringing.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade investigation design teaches confounding variables, and a shared family environment is the confound the eugenic family trees never controlled.

questions.question: Harry Laughlin, superintendent of the Eugenics Record Office, sent a sworn written statement to a Virginia court in 1924 in the case of Carrie Buck, a young woman held at the state colony for the 'feebleminded'. He called her family part of 'the shiftless, ignorant, and worthless class of anti-social whites of the South' and judged her condition inherited. What was his statement based on?
questions.answer: What the colony's doctors had told him
choices: What the colony's doctors had told him
His own tests of her mind at the colony
The record of her lessons kept by her school
His own talks with the Bucks' neighbours
questions.context: Laughlin had never met Carrie Buck: the historian Paul Lombardo found that his statement repeated language the colony's doctors had given him, and it was read into the record in his absence. A teacher of hers had written that she was 'very good' in 'deportment and lessons' before she was taken out of school in sixth grade to do housework. Indiana had passed the first sterilisation law in 1907, and Virginia's law of 1924, which the colony meant this case to test, followed a model law that Laughlin had drafted.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn to judge a claim by the evidence behind it, and an expert's sworn word with no observation behind it is the clearest case of evidence that is not there.

questions.question: At the hearing on Carrie Buck in 1924, a social worker said that her baby daughter, Vivian, had 'a look about it that is not quite normal'. Arthur Estabrook of the Eugenics Record Office held a coin before the baby's eyes and judged her feebleminded. The Supreme Court upheld Carrie's sterilisation in 1927, counting Vivian as a third generation. What did Vivian's school record later show?
questions.answer: A place on the honour roll in first grade
choices: A place on the honour roll in first grade
A grade skipped for her quick reading
An intelligence score in the lowest tenth
A move to a special class for slow learners
questions.context: Vivian was placed on the honour roll in April 1931, and Stephen Jay Gould, who studied her school records, called her 'a perfectly normal, quite average student'; she died of an infection at eight in 1932. A social worker's remark and a coin held before a baby of about seven months stood as the evidence for the third generation in Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes's line, 'Three generations of imbeciles are enough.' California alone sterilised about 20,000 people under such laws, and the Court has never expressly overturned the case.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches that a claim must survive later evidence, and Vivian's school record is the later evidence the eugenic judgement of a baby failed.

questions.question: Twenty doctors and three officials of Nazi Germany were tried at Nuremberg for medical experiments on prisoners of war and civilians, many of whom died. The three American judges set out ten principles for experiments on people in their verdict of August 1947. The first principle opens with a single sentence. What does that sentence call absolutely essential?
questions.answer: The voluntary consent of the person tested
choices: The voluntary consent of the person tested
Tests on animals before any test on people
Results that no other method could give
A risk no greater than the good it may do
questions.context: The first principle opens 'The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential' and goes on that the person must be free of 'force, fraud, deceit, duress' and know enough for 'an understanding and enlightened decision', a duty that falls on every person who starts, directs or works on the experiment. Animal tests first, results no other method can give and a risk no greater than the problem's importance are the Code's third, second and sixth principles. Several of the accused had argued that no law marked off a lawful experiment from an unlawful one; the Code itself was never made a law, but later codes of research ethics were modelled on it.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science includes the safe and ethical conduct of research, and the Nuremberg Code's first principle is the root of informed consent.

questions.question: The fifth of the ten principles that the Nuremberg judges set out in 1947 bars any experiment on people where there is reason to expect, beforehand, that death or disabling injury will follow. The judges added a single exception to it, hedged with the word 'perhaps'. Which experiments does the exception cover?
questions.answer: Those whose experimenting doctors are subjects too
choices: Those whose experimenting doctors are subjects too
Those whose subjects are prisoners condemned to die
Those whose subjects already have a deadly disease
Those whose subjects are well paid for the risk
questions.context: The fifth principle ends 'except, perhaps, in those experiments where the experimental physicians also serve as subjects': the only people the judges would let run such a risk were the researchers themselves, and even then only perhaps. The Code makes no exception for condemned prisoners, for the gravely ill or for pay. Its ninth principle adds that a subject must be free to bring an experiment to an end, and its tenth that the scientist in charge must be ready to stop it.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science includes the ethics of risk in research, and the self-experimenter exception shows how the Code ties any grave risk to the researcher's own consent.
